Hamstrings often strain at speed, right as the muscle lengthens. Kicking and changing direction also lean on the inner thigh, and both cop it more when training load jumps in pre-season.

Hybi's tip: bridge with a cushion squeeze, 3 seconds, 10 reps, 2–3 times a week. Clinical Pilates usually works well as an add-on to your running and gym work, not a swap.

Tennis loads the same spots over and over: grip through the forearm, serving through the back of the shoulder, footwork through the calves. Remedial massage can help those areas feel looser, though the effect is usually short-term.

Hybi's plan: lighter massage a day or two before a tournament, deeper work after. Pair it with calf raises and forearm and shoulder strength work so your body copes with more hitting.

caption:
Can massage really 'release' your ITB? Not quite, and that's fine.

The iliotibial band is a thick, strong band of tissue down the outside of the thigh. It doesn't stretch much, so no amount of pressure will lengthen it. What massage can do is ease tension in the muscles around it: the glutes, the front of the hip, the quads and the hamstrings.

Steady, comfortable pressure usually beats gritting your teeth. Pair it with hip and glute strength and sensible changes to your running or riding load.

caption:
Momo does squats every day, yet one leg still wobbles on the stairs.

Walking, stairs and running mostly happen on one leg at a time. In two-leg moves like a squat, the stronger side can quietly take more of the load, which is why clinical Pilates often works one side at a time, building strength and balance together.

Hybi's 1-minute check: single-leg sit-to-stand from a high chair, 6–8 reps per side, holding a bench if needed. Notice which side feels harder.

Small differences are normal. A clearly weaker leg after an injury, or pain during single-leg work, is worth an assessment first. Book online via the link in bio
